texts: good. the individual copular predication lands cleanly, with the apprentice role and the separate "new" property both on record and nothing invented for the name.

bad: "from down the coast" cannot be recorded at all — the translator has no way to carry "down" on an origin, so rather than assert the false "arrived from the coast" it has to drop the origin claim entirely, and where she came from is lost. Give the origin a noun of its own and let "down the coast" modify that noun: "Coraline Ash arrived in late summer from a place down the coast." If the place has a name in your lore, using it ("... from Ellum, a village down the coast") parses best of all. "In late summer" itself comes through fine.

good. adjudicated acceptable: the family, its link to Coraline Ash, and the habitual farming at the coast are all recorded; only the directional force of "down" goes unkept, and nothing false is asserted.
good. the denial covers exactly the right bundle — she is not from any Keeper family — while the Keeper-family kind itself stays on record outside the denial.
good. both the voting and the accepting are recorded with the Council as the doer of each, and nothing wrongly claims the acceptance already took place.

bad: the noun "acceptance" is relabelled with its verb "accept", so the thing Old Vesh supported loses its own identity in the record, and a bare event-noun object also leaves it unsaid whether the acceptance ever actually happened. Say it with a finite clause instead: "The Council accepted Coraline Ash, and Old Vesh supported that." — the "that" points back at the accepting, so the support link survives and the acceptance is stated as a real past event.
